1.title: Vulnerability Types and Attack Surfaces
1.text: Welcome to Module six: Vulnerability Types and Attack Surfaces. It covers the exam area Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Attacks. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Groups of vulnerabilities. Product and system weaknesses. Application and code vulnerabilities. Configuration, data and identity exposure. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Attacks (twenty-four percent). Exam format: up to ninety questions in ninety minutes; a score of seven hundred fifty on a scale of one hundred to nine hundred passes. Validated against: the official Comp T I A Security plus S Y zero eight oh one V eight exam objectives.

1.title: Groups of vulnerabilities
1.text: Groups of vulnerabilities. The figure shows this: Vulnerability types grouped: products and systems, software, configuration, credentials, devices and data.

1.title: Groups of vulnerabilities, continued
1.text: Groups of vulnerabilities. Products and systems. Unsupported products, unpatched systems, obsolete systems, unmanaged systems. Exposure. Ports and services left open, shadow I T, rogue devices. Software and code. Applications, code, operating system (O S)-based, virtualization, zero-day, cryptographic vulnerabilities. Configuration and data. Misconfiguration, public repositories, public object storage. Identity. Unmanaged or stale credentials, identity providers. Devices and communication. Mobile devices, wireless and low-powered communications. New in V eight. Large language models (L L Ms) as a surface.

1.title: Product and system weaknesses
1.text: Product and system weaknesses. Unsupported product. Why it is dangerous: The vendor no longer issues patches (end of life). Fix: Replace or isolate. Unpatched system. Why it is dangerous: A known fix has not been applied. Fix: Patch management. Obsolete system. Why it is dangerous: Old design, cannot meet modern controls. Fix: Retire, replace or compensate. Unmanaged system. Why it is dangerous: Not in inventory, no updates or monitoring. Fix: Asset inventory, enrollment.

1.title: Product and system weaknesses, continued
1.text: Product and system weaknesses. Open ports and services. Why it is dangerous: Unneeded listening services widen the surface. Fix: Close or disable; hardening. Shadow I T. Why it is dangerous: Tools and cloud services used without I T approval. Fix: Discovery, policy, approved alternatives. Rogue device. Why it is dangerous: An unauthorized device on the network. Fix: Network access control, scanning. Exam tip: Zero-day equals the flaw is unknown to the vendor and has no patch. End-of-life software is unsupported. A device nobody tracks is unmanaged. Fix the surface by removing what is not needed.

1.title: Application and code vulnerabilities
1.text: Application and code vulnerabilities. Race condition. The result depends on timing of events; time-of-check (T O C) to time-of-use (T O U) flaws let data change between the check and the use. Malicious update. An update that contains malware. Hardcoded secrets. Passwords or keys written in source code. Unsafe exception handling. Errors that reveal information or leave the system in an insecure state. O S-based. Flaws in the operating system itself. Virtualization. V M escape, hypervisor flaws, V M sprawl. Cryptographic vulnerabilities. Weak algorithms, short keys, bad key management. Exam tip: Fix a vulnerability by removing the cause: patch or replace unsupported software, close unused ports, review stale credentials.

1.title: Configuration, data and identity exposure
1.text: Configuration, data and identity exposure. Misconfiguration. Wrong settings, such as default passwords or open permissions. Public repositories. Code repositories that expose secrets (keys, tokens). Public object storage. Cloud storage buckets open to everyone. Unmanaged or stale credentials. Old accounts, shared passwords and service accounts nobody reviews. Identity providers. A weakness at the I D P can affect every connected application. Mobile devices. Loss, theft, jailbreaking, unmanaged apps. Wireless and low-powered communications. Weak encryption, interception, and devices with little built-in security. L L Ms. Prompt injection, data leaks and unsafe output (module eight). Exam tip: Hardcoded secrets in a public repository are a common cause of cloud breaches. An open object storage bucket is a misconfiguration. Stale accounts are found by access reviews.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Fabrikam Outdoors discovers that a developer committed a cloud access key to a public code repository. Which vulnerabilities does this show? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Hardcoded secrets exposed in a public repository. Secrets stored in code and published in a public repository are exposed for anyone to use.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A vendor announces that a server product will no longer receive security updates. How is this product described? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Unsupported. A product that no longer gets patches is unsupported (end of life).

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A flaw is being exploited, and the vendor has not yet released a patch because it was unaware. What is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: A zero-day vulnerability. A flaw unknown to the vendor with no patch available is a zero-day.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A team uses an unapproved file-sharing service to exchange customer data. Which term fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Shadow I T. Technology used without the approval or knowledge of I T is shadow I T.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A check confirms a file's permissions and then a different file replaces it before the file is opened. Which flaw is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Time-of-check to time-of-use race condition. The state changed between the check and the use, a classic T O C or T O U race condition.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Which action best reduces the exposure from unneeded open ports and services on a server? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Disable the services that are not required. Removing unneeded listening services shrinks the attack surface.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What is a zero-day vulnerability? Answer: A flaw unknown to the vendor with no patch yet. Question two. What does T O C or T O U stand for? Answer: Time-of-check and time-of-use, a race condition. Question three. What is shadow I T? Answer: Technology used without I T approval.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Give two examples of misconfiguration. Answer: Default passwords and public object storage. Question five. What is a rogue device? Answer: An unauthorized device connected to the network. Question six. Why are stale credentials risky? Answer: Old or unused accounts can be abused and nobody notices.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Systems: unsupported, unpatched, obsolete, unmanaged; open ports and services; shadow I T; rogue devices. Code: race conditions (T O C or T O U), malicious update, hardcoded secrets, unsafe exceptions, O S flaws, virtualization, weak cryptography, zero-day. Exposure: misconfiguration, public repositories, public object storage, stale credentials, identity providers, mobile and wireless, L L Ms. In the next module, we continue the course.
